items.title: 5 Mind-Blowing Facts About Honeybees
items.premise: Did you know that a single worker honeybee produces less than a drop of honey in its entire lifetime? Here are 5 astonishing, verified facts with real numbers that show how incredible these tiny insects truly are.
facts: A honeybee beats its wings 200 times per second to create its distinct buzzing sound.
During its entire 30-to-60-day lifetime, an individual worker bee produces only 1/12th of a teaspoon of honey.
To make just 1 pound (0.45 kg) of honey, a bee colony must visit roughly 2 million flowers.
A colony travels a combined distance of 55,000 miles (88,500 km) to collect enough nectar for 1 pound of honey.
Queen bees can lay up to 2,000 eggs per day during peak spring season, equal to her own body weight in eggs daily.
Honeybees use a complex 'waggle dance' to communicate exact coordinates of flower patches up to 3 miles (5 km) away.
A healthy beehive population peaks between 20,000 and 80,000 individual bees during early summer.
Archeologists found 3,000-year-old honey inside ancient Egyptian tombs that remains completely edible due to its low moisture content and acidic pH level between 3.2 and 4.5.

items.title: Trapped 700 Meters Underground: The 2010 Chilean Miner Rescue
items.premise: On August 5, 2010, a massive cave-in trapped 33 miners deep under the Atacama Desert. For 69 grueling days, they survived brutal heat and starvation until an unprecedented global engineering feat pulled every single man out alive.
facts: On August 5, 2010, a 700,000-ton rock collapse trapped 33 miners 700 meters (2,300 ft) underground in the San José Mine.
The underground shelter environment averaged 35°C (95°F) with 90% relative humidity.
The emergency shelter originally contained only 3 days worth of food rations for 33 men.
Miners rationed food down to 2 spoonfuls of canned tuna, a sip of milk, and half a cracker every 48 hours.
On Day 17 (August 22, 2010), a probe drill broke into the refuge and brought up a note attached to the bit: 'Estamos bien en el refugio los 33'.
Engineers drilled a rescue shaft 66 centimeters (26 inches) wide through solid granite.
The custom steel rescue capsule, named Fénix 2, made 39 total trips up and down the narrow shaft.
On October 13, 2010, after 69 days underground, all 33 miners were brought to the surface safely in an operation lasting 22 hours and 37 minutes.
An estimated 1 billion people watched the live rescue broadcast around the globe.
